extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of political philosophy/theology; scholars of Hobbes/early-modern political theology
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and explicating Hobbes's definitions, distinctions, and standards for religious-political terms (e.g., kingdom of God, holy, sacrament, word of God, prophet) as given in Leviathan. The passage supplies conceptual criteria and interpretive guidance used to judge meaning and authority in scripture and polity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kingdome of God as civil commonwealth
rubrics_metrics.description: The Kingdome of God is properly meant a Common-wealth, instituted (by the consent of those which were to be subject thereto) for their Civil Government, regulating behaviour towards God, one another (justice), and other Nations in peace and war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supported by scriptural citations (e.g., Exodus, Samuel, Isaiah, Micah, Ezekiel, Luke, Acts); examples: God was their King before Saul; Christ's reign is restoration of that earthly kingdom; 'Thy Kingdome come' in the Lord's Prayer refers to restoration of God's civil rule by covenant and Christ. The Kingdome is a real, not metaphoric, kingdom exercised on Earth through vicars (High Priest, later priests/kings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation and interpretation caution (Kingdom/priests phrasing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beware translations that change 'Regnum Sacerdotale' to 'Kingdome of Priests' or similar, since such renderings may obscure the literal meaning that supports ecclesiastical government by Christian kings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes criticizes translations that lessen the literal 'sacerdotall kingdom' reading because they reduce the apparent right of ecclesiastical government; translators may alter sense to protect political interests. Prefer readings consistent with parallel texts (e.g., St. Peter) and with institutional practice (High Priest sole in Sanctum Sanctorum).

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of HOLY (proper sense)
rubrics_metrics.description: Holy signifies that which is God's by special, not by general Right — i.e., set apart for his especial service (propriety obtained by consent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Jews were 'a Holy Nation' because they became God's propriety by covenant; Sabbath, Temple, sacrifices, priests are 'holy' in that propriety sense. Thus 'holy' corresponds to what is 'public' or belonging to the public person (the sovereign).

rubrics_metrics.name: Profane = Common; Holy = Proper/Public analogy
rubrics_metrics.description: The word Profane in Scripture is usually equivalent to Common; correspondingly, Holy and Proper in the Kingdome of God map to what men call Public (that which belongs to the sovereign/commonwealth).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figurative uses may call pious people 'holy' for their devout lives, but properly the term designates appropriation to God's public use. 'Hallowed be thy name' is a prayer to keep the commandment of having no other gods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degrees of Sanctity (hierarchical set-apartness)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are degrees of holiness: something set apart for God's service can be further set apart for nearer/more especial service (e.g., nation → tribe of Levi → Levites → priests → High Priest; land → city → temple → sanctum sanctorum).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this hierarchical model to judge relative sanctity and the specialness of offices/places; the most holy (e.g., High Priest, Sanctum Sanctorum) is set apart above others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a SACRAMENT
rubrics_metrics.description: A SACRAMENT is a separation of some visible thing from common use and a consecration of it to God's service, as a sign either of admission into the Kingdome of God or for commemoration of that admission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes sacraments of admission (used once; Old Testament: circumcision; New Testament: baptism) from sacraments of commemoration (reiterated; Old Testament: Passover; New Testament: Lord's Supper). Other consecrations may be called sacraments insofar as they consecrate to God's service, but as oaths of allegiance the principal sacraments are those named. Use frequency (once vs repeated) to decide admission vs commemoration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word of God defined as Sermo (speech/discourse)
rubrics_metrics.description: When mentioning 'Word of God' it does not mean a mere vocable (single word) but a perfect Speech or Discourse (Sermo/Logos) by which a speaker affirms, denies, commands, promises, threatens, wishes, or interrogates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish 'word' in grammatical sense (vocabulum) from 'word' as meaningful discourse; the latter is the relevant sense for theology and scriptural interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word of God (doctrine/subject) — scripture as Word
rubrics_metrics.description: The Word of God is often used to mean the Doctrine of Religion (Theologia); in this sense the whole scripture is the Word of God because it contains the doctrine of the Christian religion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Word of life' and 'words of this life' refer to the doctrine and teaching of Christ; 'the Word of the Gospel' = doctrine of the Kingdom. Interpret 'word' in context to decide whether it denotes spoken words or doctrinal content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word of God (as effect/thing promised)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes 'the Word of God' denotes the effect or thing itself which was affirmed, commanded, threatened, or promised — e.g., 'his word was come' meaning the foretold thing has come to pass.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scriptural usage: 'my Words shall not pass away' means the promises/prophecies will be fulfilled. Use context to read 'word' as promise/result rather than mere utterance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word of God (as reason/equity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Occasionally Scripture calls words consonant with reason and equity 'the Word of God' even when spoken by non-prophets (e.g., Pharaoh Necho's advice to Josiah read as from God).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where Scripture attributes 'word' to human speech that aligns with reason or equity, treat it as acceptable divine communication in a broader sense; this supports treating some moral/reasonable dictates as 'of God'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple acceptions of PROPHET
rubrics_metrics.description: The name PROPHET can mean (a) prolocutor — one who speaks from God to man or man to God; (b) praedictor — a foreteller of things to come; (c) one who speaks incoherently (mad speech) — all depending on context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: High Priest functioned as prophet (prolocutor); poets and hymn-makers were called 'vates' (prophets) in pagan usage; Christian congregational teachers/ prayer-leaders could be termed prophets in certain senses. Interpret 'prophet' by role and function in given passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prediction (praediction) is not identical with true Prophecy
rubrics_metrics.description: When prophecy is taken as mere prediction, impostors—those using familiar spirits or divination—may appear prophetic; true prophecy is an extraordinary temporary employment from God, not a reliable art or constant vocation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of confounding coincidence or divinatory arts with genuine prophecy; Hobbes notes imposters can gain reputation by one chance success but lose it by many failures. Use origin (divine commission vs. human technique) and moral character as distinguishing marks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of God's speaking to prophets (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: God makes his will known to prophets by various ways; for extraordinary prophets in Old Testament the usual modes were Dreams, Visions, and Apparitions; in the New Testament similar modes occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Abraham, Jacob, Moses (burning bush), Gideon, Samuel, Elijah, Elisha, Isaiah, Ezekiel — all received visions or dreams; Joseph, Peter, Paul, John had visions or dreams. Use the record of signs (visions, dreams, apparitions) to identify divine speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moses and High Priests as exceptional recipients of divine speech
rubrics_metrics.description: To Moses God spake in a more extraordinary manner — 'mouth to mouth, even apparently' — and to the High Priest from the Mercy Seat in a manner not fully expressed in Scripture; these cases differ qualitatively from dreams/visions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not reduce Moses' or the High Priest's reception to ordinary dream/vision categories; their communication is uniquely close and is treated as authoritative and supra-ordinary in Hobbes's account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophets of perpetual calling: supreme vs subordinate
rubrics_metrics.description: Among prophets with perpetual calling some were supreme (Moses, the High Priest, pious kings) and some subordinate; subordinate prophets' revelations were subordinate to and derived from the supreme prophet's authority; 'Spirit' in subordinate cases often denotes inclination or grace, not substantial divine indwelling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use institutional relations to judge prophetic authority: subordinate prophets act under commission or derivation from supreme prophetic authority (e.g., seventy elders given Moses' spirit); 'speaking in the Spirit' often means speaking according to God's will as declared by the supreme prophet, not literal possession of the divine nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: God may speak by lots (divine will via chance events)
rubrics_metrics.description: God sometimes declared his will by the event of lots cast by those in authority (e.g., land division by Joshua, detection of crime by lots).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize lots as one of the Biblical means attributed to divine decision; when scripture reports lots with interpretive authority, treat the result as an expression of God's will mediated through human procedure.
